nodes.name: Rank of a tensor
nodes.statement: A non-zero tensor corresponding to an element of $V_1\otimes \cdots\otimes V_d$ of the form $\aaa_1\otimes\cdots\otimes \aaa_d$ is called a rank 1 tensor. For a general tensor $T$ of format $N_1\times\cdots\times N_d$, the rank of $T$, denoted by $\rank T$, is by definition the minimum integer $r$ such that $T$ can be expressed as a sum of $r$ rank 1 tensors, where we set the empty sum to be zero.
nodes.statement_short: Rank of a tensor is the minimum number of rank-1 tensors summing to it.
differentia: such that $T$ can be expressed as a sum of $r$ rank 1 tensors

nodes.name: Generic rank $\grank_\CCC(p,n,m)$
nodes.statement: If the base field is $\CCC$, the set of tensors of format $p\times n\times m$ with rank at most $r$ contains a non-empty Zariski open set if and only if its Zariski closure is $\CCC^{p\times n\times m}$ (cf., Chevalley's Theorem, see e.g., \cite[p.\ 39]{har92}). Therefore, there exists exactly one ``typical rank of $p\times n\times m$ tensors over $\CCC$''. This is called the generic rank of $p\times n\times m$ tensors over $\CCC$ and denoted as $\grank_\CCC(p,n,m)$ or simply $\grank(p,n,m)$.
nodes.statement_short: Over $\CCC$ there is a unique typical rank, called the generic rank.
nodes.definiendum: the generic rank of $p\times n\times m$ tensors over $\CCC$

nodes.name: Semi-tall tensor
nodes.statement: Here we define a $p\times n\times m$-tensor a semi-tall tensor if $(m-1)(n-1)+1\leq p\leq (m-1)n$.

nodes.name: Nonsingular bilinear map
nodes.statement: where a bilinear map $\varphi\colon V_1\times V_2\to W$ is \nonsing\ if $\varphi(x,y)=0$ implies $x=0$ or $y=0$.
nodes.origin_citation: Sumi, Sakata & Miyazaki 2013; Sumi, Miyazaki & Sakata 2015, 2017

nodes.name: Plurality of typical ranks for $p=(m-1)(n-1)+1$ with no nonsingular bilinear map
nodes.statement: Therefore, the case where $p=(m-1)(n-1)+1$ and there is no \nonsing\ bilinear map $\RRR^m\times\RRR^n\to\RRR^u$ is still left open.
nodes.statement_short: Open: are there plural typical ranks when $p=(m-1)(n-1)+1$ and no nonsingular bilinear map exists?
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$

nodes.name: Typical rank $\trank_\RRR(\ell,m,n)$
nodes.statement: If the set of rank $r$ tensors over $\RRR$ of format $\ell\times m\times n$ contains a non-empty Euclidean open subset of $\RRR^{\ell\times m\times n}$, then we say $r$ is a typical rank of $\ell\times m\times n$ tensors over $\RRR$. We denote the set of typical ranks of $\ell\times m\times n$ tensors over $\RRR$ by $\trank_\RRR(\ell,m,n)$ or simply $\trank(\ell,m,n)$.
nodes.statement_short: $r$ is a typical rank if the rank-$r$ tensors contain a non-empty Euclidean open set.
nodes.origin_citation: standard notion; cf. Sakata, Sumi & Miyazaki 2016
nodes.definiendum: a typical rank of $\ell\times m\times n$ tensors over $\RRR$
differentia: the set of rank $r$ tensors over $\RRR$ of format $\ell\times m\times n$ contains a non-empty Euclidean open subset of $\RRR^{\ell\times m\times n}$

nodes.name: Permutation invariance of typical ranks
nodes.statement: Let $n_1$, $n_2$ and $n_3$ be positive integers. Then $\trank(n_{i_1},n_{i_2},n_{i_3})=\trank(n_1,n_2,n_3)$ for any permutation $i_1$, $i_2$, $i_3$ of 1, 2, 3.
nodes.statement_short: The set of typical ranks is invariant under permuting the three format dimensions.

nodes.name: Flattenings $\fl_1(T)$ and $\fl_2(T)$
nodes.statement: For $T=(T_1;\cdots;T_n)\in K^{\ell\times m\times n}$, we set $$ \fl_1(T)\define(T_1,\ldots, T_n)\in K^{\ell\times mn} $$ and $$ \fl_2(T)\define \begin{pmatrix}T_1\\\vdots\\T_n\end{pmatrix}\in K^{\ell n\times m} $$ and call flattenings of $T$.
nodes.statement_short: Two matrix flattenings of a 3-tensor, unfolding along the first and second modes.

nodes.name: Truncation notation $M_{\leq j}$, ${}_{j<}M$, $M^{\leq i}$, ${}^{i<}M$
nodes.statement: For $M=(\mmm_1,\ldots,\mmm_n)= \begin{pmatrix}\mmm^{(1)}\\\vdots\\\mmm^{(\ell)}\end{pmatrix} \in K^{\ell\times n}$, we set $M_{\leq j}\define(\mmm_1,\ldots, \mmm_{j})$, ${}_{j<}M\define(\mmm_{j+1},\ldots, \mmm_{n})$, $M^{\leq i}\define\begin{pmatrix}\mmm^{(1)}\\\vdots\\\mmm^{(i)}\end{pmatrix}$ and ${}^{i<}M\define\begin{pmatrix}\mmm^{(i+1)}\\\vdots\\\mmm^{(\ell)}\end{pmatrix}$.
nodes.statement_short: Notation for the leading/trailing column and row blocks of a matrix.

nodes.name: Ideal of $t$-minors $I_t(M)$
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $M\in R^{\ell\times n}$. We denote by $I_t(M)$ the ideal of $R$ generated by $t$-minors of $R$.

nodes.name: Standing hypotheses on $m$, $n$, $p$ and $u=mn-p$
nodes.statement: From now on, let $m$, $n$ and $p$ be integers with $3\leq m\leq n$ and $(m-1)(n-1)+1\leq p\leq mn$. We set $u=mn-p$.
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$

nodes.name: Known results on typical ranks of semi-tall tensors
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item $\grank(p,n,m)=p$. In particular, $\min\trank(p,n,m)=p$ \cite{cgg02}. \item If $p>(m-1)n$, then $\trank(p,n,m)=\{p\}$ \cite{tb00}. \item Suppose $p\leq (m-1)n$. If there exists a \nonsing\ bilinear map $\RRR^m\times\RRR^n\to\RRR^u$, then $\trank(p,n,m)=\{p,p+1\}$. Moreover, if $(m-1)(n-1)+2\leq p$, then the converse also hold true \cite{ssm13,sms15, sms17}. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Recap: $\grank=p$; $\trank=\{p\}$ for tall tensors; $\trank=\{p,p+1\}$ iff a nonsingular bilinear map exists (for $p\geq(m-1)(n-1)+2$).
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$
nodes.origin_citation: Catalisano, Geramita & Gimigliano 2002; ten Berge 2000; Sumi, Sakata & Miyazaki 2013, 2015, 2017
assumptions: let $m$, $n$ and $p$ be integers with $3\leq m\leq n$ and $(m-1)(n-1)+1\leq p\leq mn$.

nodes.name: The linear matrix pencil $M(\xxx,A)$
nodes.statement: Let $\xxx=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)$ be a row vector of indeterminates, i.e., $x_1$, \ldots, $x_m$ are independent indeterminates. For $A=(A_1;\cdots;A_m)\in\RRR^{u\times n\times m}$, we set $M(\xxx,A)\define x_1A_1+\cdots+x_mA_m\in \RRR[x_1, \ldots, x_m]^{u\times n}$.
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$

nodes.name: $\psi(\aaa,\bbb)$ and the subspace $U(Y)$
nodes.statement: Let $\aaa$ and $\bbb$ be column vectors with entries in $\RRR$ of dimension $m$ and $n$ respectively. We set $\psi(\aaa,\bbb)\define(\aaa\kprod\bbb)^{\leq p}$, where $\kprod$ denotes the Kronecker product, i.e., if $\aaa=\begin{pmatrix}a_1\\\vdots\\ a_m\end{pmatrix}$, then $\psi(\aaa,\bbb)= \begin{pmatrix}a_1\bbb\\\vdots\\ a_{m-2}\bbb\\ a_{m-1}\bbb^{\leq p-(m-2)n}\end{pmatrix}$. For $Y\in\RRR^{u\times n\times m}$, we define $U(Y)$ to be the vector subspace of $\RRR^p$ generated by $\{\psi(\aaa,\bbb)\mid M(\aaa\transpose,Y)\bbb=\zerovec\}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\psi$ truncates the Kronecker product $\aaa\otimes\bbb$ to $p$ entries; $U(Y)$ is the span of the $\psi$-images of the kernel pairs of $M(\aaa^\top,Y)$.
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$

nodes.name: Rank-$p$ criterion via $\dim U(\mu(\sigma(T)))$
nodes.statement: For $T\in\msVVV$, $\rank T=p$ if and only if $\dim U(\mu(\sigma(T)))=p$.
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$
conclusions: $\rank T=p$ if and only if $\dim U(\mu(\sigma(T)))=p$.

nodes.name: Proof of the rank-$p$ criterion
nodes.statement: Set $\mu(\sigma(T))=W=(W_1;\cdots;W_m)$ and $\ell=u-n$. Then by \cite[Theorem 6.5 (1)$\iff$(3)]{sms17}, we see that $\rank T=p$ if and only if there are $B=(\bbb_1, \ldots, \bbb_p)\in\RRR^{n\times p}$ and $p\times p$ diagonal matrices $D_1$, \ldots, $D_m$ such that $$ (\ast) \left\{ \begin{array}{lll} D_k=\diag(d_{1k},\ldots, d_{pk})&\mbox{for $1\leq k\leq m$,}\\ (d_{j1}W_1+\cdots+d_{jm}W_m)\bbb_j=\zerovec&\mbox{for $1\leq j\leq p$ and}\\ \mbox{$\begin{pmatrix} BD_1\\\vdots\\BD_{m-2}\\B^{\leq n-\ell}D_{m-1}\end{pmatrix}$ is \nonsing.} \end{array} \right. $$ First suppose that there are $B=(\bbb_1, \ldots, \bbb_p)\in\RRR^{n\times p}$ and $D_1$, \ldots, $D_m$ which satisfy $(\ast)$. If we set $\aaa_j=(d_{j1},\ldots, d_{jm})\transpose$ for $1\leq j\leq p$, then $$ M(\aaa_j\transpose,W)\bbb_j=\zerovec $$ for $1\leq j\leq p$ and $$ (\psi(\aaa_1,\bbb_1), \ldots,\psi(\aaa_p,\bbb_p))= \begin{pmatrix} BD_1\\\vdots\\BD_{m-2}\\B^{\leq n-\ell}D_{m-1}\end{pmatrix} $$ is \nonsing. Therefore $\dim U(\mu(\sigma(T)))=p$. Conversely, assume that $\dim U(\mu(\sigma(T)))=p$. Then there are $\aaa_1$, \ldots, $\aaa_p\in\RRR^m$ and $\bbb_1$, \ldots, $\bbb_p\in\RRR^n$ such that $\psi(\aaa_1,\bbb_1)$, \ldots, $\psi(\aaa_p,\bbb_p)$ are linearly independent. Set $\aaa_j=(d_{j1},\ldots,d_{jm})\transpose$ for $1\leq j\leq p$, $D_k=\diag(d_{1k},\ldots,d_{pk})$ for $1\leq k\leq m$ and $B=(\bbb_1,\ldots,\bbb_p)\in\RRR^{n\times p}$. Then it is easily verified that $B$ and $D_1$, \ldots, $D_m$ satisfy $(\ast)$.
nodes.statement_short: Translate the rank condition into the system $(\ast)$ via \cite{sms17}, then match solutions of $(\ast)$ with linearly independent $\psi(\aaa_j,\bbb_j)$ in both directions.
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$

nodes.name: The system $(\ast)$
nodes.statement: $$ (\ast) \left\{ \begin{array}{lll} D_k=\diag(d_{1k},\ldots, d_{pk})&\mbox{for $1\leq k\leq m$,}\\ (d_{j1}W_1+\cdots+d_{jm}W_m)\bbb_j=\zerovec&\mbox{for $1\leq j\leq p$ and}\\ \mbox{$\begin{pmatrix} BD_1\\\vdots\\BD_{m-2}\\B^{\leq n-\ell}D_{m-1}\end{pmatrix}$ is \nonsing.} \end{array} \right. $$
nodes.statement_short: Diagonal matrices $D_k$ and vectors $\bbb_j$ with $(d_{j1}W_1+\cdots+d_{jm}W_m)\bbb_j=\zerovec$ and a nonsingular stacked matrix.
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$

nodes.name: Reduce to the system $(\ast)$
nodes.statement: Set $\mu(\sigma(T))=W=(W_1;\cdots;W_m)$ and $\ell=u-n$. Then by \cite[Theorem 6.5 (1)$\iff$(3)]{sms17}, we see that $\rank T=p$ if and only if there are $B=(\bbb_1, \ldots, \bbb_p)\in\RRR^{n\times p}$ and $p\times p$ diagonal matrices $D_1$, \ldots, $D_m$ such that $$ (\ast) \left\{ \begin{array}{lll} D_k=\diag(d_{1k},\ldots, d_{pk})&\mbox{for $1\leq k\leq m$,}\\ (d_{j1}W_1+\cdots+d_{jm}W_m)\bbb_j=\zerovec&\mbox{for $1\leq j\leq p$ and}\\ \mbox{$\begin{pmatrix} BD_1\\\vdots\\BD_{m-2}\\B^{\leq n-\ell}D_{m-1}\end{pmatrix}$ is \nonsing.} \end{array} \right. $$
nodes.statement_short: Invoke \cite[Theorem 6.5]{sms17} to restate $\rank T=p$ as solvability of $(\ast)$.
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$

nodes.name: From a solution of $(\ast)$ to $\dim U=p$
nodes.statement: First suppose that there are $B=(\bbb_1, \ldots, \bbb_p)\in\RRR^{n\times p}$ and $D_1$, \ldots, $D_m$ which satisfy $(\ast)$. If we set $\aaa_j=(d_{j1},\ldots, d_{jm})\transpose$ for $1\leq j\leq p$, then $$ M(\aaa_j\transpose,W)\bbb_j=\zerovec $$ for $1\leq j\leq p$ and $$ (\psi(\aaa_1,\bbb_1), \ldots,\psi(\aaa_p,\bbb_p))= \begin{pmatrix} BD_1\\\vdots\\BD_{m-2}\\B^{\leq n-\ell}D_{m-1}\end{pmatrix} $$ is \nonsing. Therefore $\dim U(\mu(\sigma(T)))=p$.
nodes.statement_short: Set $\aaa_j=(d_{j1},\ldots,d_{jm})^\top$ and read off that the $\psi(\aaa_j,\bbb_j)$ span $\RRR^p$.
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$

nodes.name: Converse: from $\dim U=p$ to a solution of $(\ast)$
nodes.statement: Conversely, assume that $\dim U(\mu(\sigma(T)))=p$. Then there are $\aaa_1$, \ldots, $\aaa_p\in\RRR^m$ and $\bbb_1$, \ldots, $\bbb_p\in\RRR^n$ such that $\psi(\aaa_1,\bbb_1)$, \ldots, $\psi(\aaa_p,\bbb_p)$ are linearly independent. Set $\aaa_j=(d_{j1},\ldots,d_{jm})\transpose$ for $1\leq j\leq p$, $D_k=\diag(d_{1k},\ldots,d_{pk})$ for $1\leq k\leq m$ and $B=(\bbb_1,\ldots,\bbb_p)\in\RRR^{n\times p}$. Then it is easily verified that $B$ and $D_1$, \ldots, $D_m$ satisfy $(\ast)$.
nodes.statement_short: Given $p$ independent $\psi(\aaa_j,\bbb_j)$, build $B$ and the $D_k$ satisfying $(\ast)$.
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$

nodes.name: Standing case $p=(m-1)(n-1)+1$, $u=m+n-2$
nodes.statement: From now on, we consider the case where $p=(m-1)(n-1)+1$. Then $u=m+n-2$.

nodes.name: The tensor $A=(A_1;\cdots;A_m)$
nodes.statement: We set $$ A_k\define\begin{pmatrix}O_{(k-1)\times n}\\ E_n\\ O_{(m-k-1)\times n}\end{pmatrix} \in\RRR^{u\times n} $$ for $1\leq k\leq m-1$ and $$ A_{m}\define\begin{pmatrix}O_{(m-1)\times(n-1)}&-\eee_1\\ E_{n-1}&\zerovec\end{pmatrix} \in\RRR^{u\times n}, $$ where $\eee_1=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\\vdots\\0\end{pmatrix}\in\RRR^{m-1}$ and $A=(A_1;\cdots;A_m)\in\RRR^{u\times n\times m}$.
nodes.statement_short: An explicit $u\times n\times m$ tensor built from identity blocks and a shifted block $A_m$.

nodes.name: Key Lemma
nodes.statement: Let $y$ be an indeterminate and $a_1,\ldots, a_{m-1}\in\CCC$. Then the following conditions are equivalent, where $V_a(I)$ denotes the affine variety defined by an ideal $I$. \begin{enumerate} \item $(a_1,\ldots, a_{m-1},-1)\in V_a(I_n(M(\xxx,A)))$. \item $y^{m-1}-a_{m-1}y^{m-2}-\cdots-a_2y-a_1$ is a factor of $y^u+1$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Points of the determinantal variety of $M(\xxx,A)$ correspond to degree-$(m-1)$ monic factors of $y^u+1$.
assumptions: Let $y$ be an indeterminate and $a_1,\ldots, a_{m-1}\in\CCC$.

nodes.name: The ideal $\msIII(\{\mu_t\}_{t\geq 1})$
nodes.statement: Let $y$ be an indeterminate and $\{\mu_t\}_{t\geq 1}$ an infinite sequence of complex numbers. We set $\msIII(\{\mu_t\}_{t\geq 1}) =\{f(y)\in\CCC[y]\mid f(y)=\sum_k c_k y^k$, $\sum_k c_k\mu_{k+t}=0$ for any $t\geq 1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Polynomials whose coefficients annihilate every shift of the sequence $\{\mu_t\}$.

nodes.name: $\msIII(\{\mu_t\}_{t\geq 1})$ is an ideal
nodes.statement: It is easily verified that $\msIII(\{\mu_t\}_{t\geq 1})$ is an ideal of $\CCC[y]$.

nodes.name: The sequence $\{\lambda_t\}$
nodes.statement: Now let $a_1$, \ldots, $a_{m-1}\in\CCC$. Set $\lambda_t=0$ for $1\leq t\leq m-2$, $\lambda_{m-1}=1$ and $$ \lambda_{m-1+s}= \det\begin{pmatrix} a_{m-1}&a_{m-2}&\cdots&a_1\\ -1&\ddots&\ddots&&\ddots\\ &\ddots&\ddots&\ddots&&a_1\\ &&\ddots&\ddots&\ddots&\vdots\\ &&&\ddots&\ddots&a_{m-2}\\ &&&&-1&a_{m-1} \end{pmatrix} $$ for $s\geq 1$, where the right hand side is an $s\times s$-determinant (some $a_i$'s may not appear for small $s$).
nodes.statement_short: $\lambda_t$ is a determinant of a banded $s\times s$ matrix in the $a_i$, with $\lambda_t=0$ for $t\leq m-2$ and $\lambda_{m-1}=1$.

nodes.name: Proof of the recurrence for $\lambda_t$
nodes.statement: By the first row expansion, we see the following
nodes.statement_short: First-row expansion of the determinant.

nodes.name: Recurrence relation for $\lambda_t$
nodes.statement: For $t\geq m$, we have $\lambda_t=\sum_{k=1}^{m-1}a_{m-k}\lambda_{t-k}$.

nodes.name: $\msIII(\{\lambda_t\}_{t\geq 1})$ is generated by $h(y)$
nodes.statement: By the above lemma, we see that $h(y)\in\msIII(\{\lambda_t\}_{t\geq 1})$. Further, since $\lambda_t=0$ for $1\leq t\leq m-2$ and $\lambda_{m-1}=1$, there is no polynomial in $\msIII(\{\lambda_t\}_{t\geq 1})$ whose degree is less than $m-1$ except the zero polynomial, i.e., $\msIII(\{\lambda_t\}_{t\geq 1})$ is generated by $h(y)$.
nodes.statement_short: $h(y)$ lies in the ideal and is of minimal degree, hence generates it.

nodes.name: The matrix $N$ and its maximal minors $[c_1,\ldots,c_n]_N$
nodes.statement: Set $$ N=M((a_1,\ldots, a_{m-1},-1),A) =\begin{pmatrix}a_1&&&&1\\ a_2&\ddots\\ \vdots&\ddots&\ddots\\ a_{m-1}&&\ddots&\ddots\\ -1&\ddots&&\ddots&a_1\\ &\ddots&\ddots&&a_2\\ &&\ddots&\ddots&\vdots\\ &&&-1&a_{m-1} \end{pmatrix} $$ and for integers $c_1$, \ldots, $c_n$ with $1\leq c_1<\cdots<c_n\leq u$, we denote by $[c_1, \ldots, c_n]_N$ the maximal minor of $N$ consisting of the $c_1$-th, \ldots, $c_n$-th rows of $N$.
nodes.statement_short: $N=M((a_1,\ldots,a_{m-1},-1),A)$, a banded $u\times n$ matrix, with $[c_1,\ldots,c_n]_N$ its maximal minors.

nodes.name: Equivalent conditions for $\rank N<n$
nodes.statement: Under the notation above, the following conditions are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item $\rank N<n$. \item $[i,m,m+1,\ldots,u]_N=0$ for $1\leq i\leq m-1$. \item $\lambda_{u+t}=0$ for $1\leq t\leq m-2$ and $\lambda_{u+m-1}=-1$. \item $\lambda_{u+t}=-\lambda_t$ for $t\geq 1$. \item $y^u+1\in\msIII(\{\lambda_t\}_{t\geq 1})$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Five equivalent conditions: rank drop of $N$, vanishing minors, $\lambda$-recurrence conditions, and $y^u+1\in\msIII(\{\lambda_t\})$.

nodes.name: Proof of the equivalences for $\rank N<n$
nodes.statement: Let $$ U=\begin{pmatrix} a_{m-1}&a_{m-2}&\cdots&a_1&&1\\ -1&\ddots&\ddots&&\ddots\\ &\ddots&\ddots&\ddots&&a_1\\ &&\ddots&\ddots&\ddots&\vdots\\ &&&\ddots&\ddots&a_{m-2}\\ &&&&-1&a_{m-1} \end{pmatrix} $$ be a $u\times u$ matrix. Then $\det({}^{t<}_{t<}U)=\lambda_{u+m-1-t}+\delta_{0,t}$ for $0\leq t\leq u-1$, where $\delta_{0,t}$ is the Kronecker's delta. \ref{item:rank less than n}$\Longrightarrow$\ref{item:lambda u+1}: Since ${}_{m-2<}U=N$ and $\rank N<n$ by assumption, we see that $\det({}^{t<}_{t<}U)=0$ for $0\leq t\leq m-2$. Thus, we see that $\lambda_{u+m-1-t}+\delta_{0,t}=0$ for $0\leq t\leq m-2$. \ref{item:lambda u+1}$\Longrightarrow$\ref{item:minors vanish}: We see by the first row expansions of $\det({}_{t<}^{t<}U)$ and $[t+1,m,\ldots, u]$ and the assumption that \begin{eqnarray*} 0&=&\lambda_{u+m-1-t}+\delta_{0,t}\\ &=&\sum_{k=1}^{m-1}a_{m-k}\lambda_{u+m-1-t-k}+\delta_{0,t}\\ &=&\sum_{k=m-t-1}^{m-1}a_{m-k}\lambda_{u+m-1-t-k}+\delta_{0,t}\\ &=&\sum_{s=1}^{t+1}a_{t+2-s}\lambda_{u+1-s}+\delta_{0,t}\\ &=&[t+1,m,\ldots, u]_N \end{eqnarray*} for $0\leq t\leq m-2$. \ref{item:minors vanish}$\Longrightarrow$\ref{item:rank less than n} follows from the fact that the last $n-1$ rows of $N$ are linearly independent, \ref{item:lambda u+1}$\iff$\ref{item:rec u} follows from the facts that $\lambda_1=\cdots=\lambda_{m-2}=0$ and $\lambda_{m-1}=1$ and Lemma \ref{lem:rec rel} and \ref{item:rec u}$\iff$\ref{item:yu} follows from the definition of $\msIII(\{\lambda_t\}_{t\geq 1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the $u\times u$ matrix $U$ whose corner minors are the $\lambda$'s, then close the cycle of implications (1)$\Rightarrow$(3)$\Rightarrow$(2)$\Rightarrow$(1) and read off (3)$\iff$(4)$\iff$(5).

nodes.name: Introduce the matrix $U$ and its corner minors
nodes.statement: Let $$ U=\begin{pmatrix} a_{m-1}&a_{m-2}&\cdots&a_1&&1\\ -1&\ddots&\ddots&&\ddots\\ &\ddots&\ddots&\ddots&&a_1\\ &&\ddots&\ddots&\ddots&\vdots\\ &&&\ddots&\ddots&a_{m-2}\\ &&&&-1&a_{m-1} \end{pmatrix} $$ be a $u\times u$ matrix. Then $\det({}^{t<}_{t<}U)=\lambda_{u+m-1-t}+\delta_{0,t}$ for $0\leq t\leq u-1$, where $\delta_{0,t}$ is the Kronecker's delta.
nodes.statement_short: Define $U$ and record $\det({}^{t<}_{t<}U)=\lambda_{u+m-1-t}+\delta_{0,t}$.

nodes.name: (1) implies (3)
nodes.statement: \ref{item:rank less than n}$\Longrightarrow$\ref{item:lambda u+1}: Since ${}_{m-2<}U=N$ and $\rank N<n$ by assumption, we see that $\det({}^{t<}_{t<}U)=0$ for $0\leq t\leq m-2$.
nodes.statement_short: Rank drop forces the corner minors of $U$ to vanish, giving the $\lambda_{u+t}$ conditions.

nodes.name: (3) implies (2)
nodes.statement: \ref{item:lambda u+1}$\Longrightarrow$\ref{item:minors vanish}: We see by the first row expansions of $\det({}_{t<}^{t<}U)$ and $[t+1,m,\ldots, u]$ and the assumption that \begin{eqnarray*} 0&=&\lambda_{u+m-1-t}+\delta_{0,t}\\ &=&\sum_{k=1}^{m-1}a_{m-k}\lambda_{u+m-1-t-k}+\delta_{0,t}\\ &=&\sum_{k=m-t-1}^{m-1}a_{m-k}\lambda_{u+m-1-t-k}+\delta_{0,t}\\ &=&\sum_{s=1}^{t+1}a_{t+2-s}\lambda_{u+1-s}+\delta_{0,t}\\ &=&[t+1,m,\ldots, u]_N \end{eqnarray*} for $0\leq t\leq m-2$.
nodes.statement_short: First-row expansions turn the $\lambda$ conditions into vanishing maximal minors of $N$.

nodes.name: Remaining implications
nodes.statement: \ref{item:minors vanish}$\Longrightarrow$\ref{item:rank less than n} follows from the fact that the last $n-1$ rows of $N$ are linearly independent, \ref{item:lambda u+1}$\iff$\ref{item:rec u} follows from the facts that $\lambda_1=\cdots=\lambda_{m-2}=0$ and $\lambda_{m-1}=1$ and Lemma \ref{lem:rec rel} and \ref{item:rec u}$\iff$\ref{item:yu} follows from the definition of $\msIII(\{\lambda_t\}_{t\geq 1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Close the cycle with the independence of the last $n-1$ rows, and get (3)$\iff$(4)$\iff$(5) from the recurrence and the definition of $\msIII$.

nodes.name: Proof of the Key Lemma
nodes.statement: Since $(a_1,\ldots, a_{m-1},-1)\in V_a(I_n(M(\xxx,A)))$ if and only if $\rank N<n$ and $y^u+1\in\msIII(\{\lambda_t\}_{t\geq 1})$ if and only if $h(y)$ divides $y^u+1$, we see Lemma \ref{lem:key} by Lemma \ref{lem:non full rank}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the two reformulations with the rank-drop equivalences of the previous lemma.

nodes.name: Degree and codimension of the determinantal variety
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a $u\times n$ matrix of indeterminates. Then the projective variety in $\PPP_\CCC\CCC^{u\times n}$ defined by $I_n(X)$ has degree ${u\choose n-1}$ and codimension $u-n+1$.
assumptions: Let $X$ be a $u\times n$ matrix of indeterminates.
conclusions: the projective variety in $\PPP_\CCC\CCC^{u\times n}$ defined by $I_n(X)$ has degree ${u\choose n-1}$ and codimension $u-n+1$.

nodes.name: Matching counts: ${u\choose m-1}$ factors
nodes.statement: Note that ${u\choose n-1}={u\choose m-1}$ and $u-n+1=m-1$ since $u=m+n-2$. Note also that there are ${u\choose m-1}$ monic factors of $y^u+1$ of degree $m-1$ in $\CCC[y]$.
nodes.statement_short: The degree of the determinantal variety equals the number of monic degree-$(m-1)$ factors of $y^u+1$.
conclusions: there are ${u\choose m-1}$ monic factors of $y^u+1$ of degree $m-1$ in $\CCC[y]$.

nodes.name: The map $\varphi_B$
nodes.statement: For $B=(B_1;\cdots; B_m)\in\CCC^{u\times n\times m}$, we set $\varphi_B\colon\CCC^m\to\CCC^{u\times n}$, $(\alpha_1,\ldots, \alpha_m)\mapsto\alpha_1B_1+\cdots+\alpha_mB_m$.

nodes.name: Proof of the transversality corollary
nodes.statement: Then by Lemma \ref{lem:key}, Fact \ref{fac:deg} and Bezout's theorem, we see the following
nodes.statement_short: Key Lemma, degree fact and Bezout.

nodes.name: Transverse intersection at ${u\choose m-1}$ points
nodes.statement: Let $\PPP_\CCC(\image\varphi_A)$ be the linear subspace of $\PPP_\CCC\CCC^{u\times n}$ defined by $\image\varphi_A$. Then $\PPP_\CCC(\image\varphi_A)$ and $V_p(I_n(X))$ intersect transversely at ${u\choose m-1}$ distinct points, where $V_p(I)$ denotes the projective variety defined by the homogeneous ideal $I$.
nodes.statement_short: The linear space $\PPP_\CCC(\image\varphi_A)$ meets the determinantal variety transversely in ${u\choose m-1}$ points.
assumptions: Let $\PPP_\CCC(\image\varphi_A)$ be the linear subspace of $\PPP_\CCC\CCC^{u\times n}$ defined by $\image\varphi_A$.
conclusions: $\PPP_\CCC(\image\varphi_A)$ and $V_p(I_n(X))$ intersect transversely at ${u\choose m-1}$ distinct points

nodes.name: Proof of the stability corollary
nodes.statement: By the implicit function theorem, we see the following fact.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the implicit function theorem.

nodes.name: Stable neighborhood $\msUUU$ of $A$
nodes.statement: There is a Euclidean open neighborhood $\msUUU$ of $A$ in $\RRR^{u\times n\times m}$ such that if $B\in\msUUU$, then $\varphi_B$ is injective and the number of real points of $V_p(I_n(M(\xxx,B)))\subset\PPP_\CCC\CCC^m$ is the number of real monic polynomials of degree $m-1$ which divide $y^u+1$, where we say a point of a complex projective space is real if all possible ratios of its homogeneous coordintes are real numbers.
nodes.statement_short: Near $A$, the count of real points of the determinantal variety equals the number of real monic degree-$(m-1)$ divisors of $y^u+1$.
conclusions: There is a Euclidean open neighborhood $\msUUU$ of $A$ in $\RRR^{u\times n\times m}$
$\varphi_B$ is injective and the number of real points of $V_p(I_n(M(\xxx,B)))\subset\PPP_\CCC\CCC^m$ is the number of real monic polynomials of degree $m-1$ which divide $y^u+1$

nodes.name: $\alpha(m,n)$
nodes.statement: We denote the number of real monic polynomials of degree $m-1$ which divides $y^u+1$ by $\alpha(m,n)$.
nodes.genus: the number of real monic polynomials of degree $m-1$

nodes.name: Closed formula for $\alpha(m,n)$
nodes.statement: $$ \alpha(m,n)= \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} {u/2\choose (m-1)/2}&\quad\mbox{if $m$ and $n$ are odd,}\\ {(u-1)/2\choose (m-2)/2}&\quad\mbox{if $m$ is even and $n$ is odd,}\\ {(u-1)/2\choose (m-1)/2}&\quad\mbox{if $m$ is odd and $n$ is even and}\\ 0&\quad\mbox{if $m$ and $n$ are even.} \end{array} \right. $$
nodes.statement_short: $\alpha(m,n)$ is a binomial coefficient depending on the parities of $m$ and $n$, and vanishes when both are even.
assumptions: We denote the number of real monic polynomials of degree $m-1$ which divides $y^u+1$ by $\alpha(m,n)$.
conclusions: $$ \alpha(m,n)= \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} {u/2\choose (m-1)/2}&\quad\mbox{if $m$ and $n$ are odd,}\\ {(u-1)/2\choose (m-2)/2}&\quad\mbox{if $m$ is even and $n$ is odd,}\\ {(u-1)/2\choose (m-1)/2}&\quad\mbox{if $m$ is odd and $n$ is even and}\\ 0&\quad\mbox{if $m$ and $n$ are even.} \end{array} \right. $$

nodes.name: Shrinking $\msUUU$ to keep $\rank(M(\aaa,B)_{\leq n-1})=n-1$
nodes.statement: By replacing $\msUUU$ to a smaller neighborhood if necessary, we may assume that $\rank (M(\aaa,B)_{\leq n-1})=n-1$ for any $B\in\msUUU$ and $\aaa\in\RRR^m\setminus\{\zerovec\}$ (cf.\ \cite[Corollary 4.20]{sms17}).
nodes.statement_short: WLOG every $B\in\msUUU$ has $M(\aaa,B)_{\leq n-1}$ of full rank $n-1$ for all nonzero $\aaa$.

nodes.name: Number of generators $\psi(\aaa,\bbb)$ for $B\in\msUUU$
nodes.statement: Suppose $B\in\msUUU$. Then $\#\{[\psi(\aaa,\bbb)]\in\PPP_\RRR\RRR^p\mid M(\aaa,B)\bbb=\zerovec, \aaa\in\RRR^m\setminus\{\zerovec\}, \bbb\in\RRR^n\setminus\{\zerovec\}\} =\alpha(m,n)$, where $[\xxx]$ denotes the point of $\PPP_\RRR\RRR^p$ defined by $\xxx\in\RRR^p\setminus\{\zerovec\}$.
nodes.statement_short: For $B$ near $A$ there are exactly $\alpha(m,n)$ projective points $[\psi(\aaa,\bbb)]$ with $M(\aaa,B)\bbb=\zerovec$.

nodes.name: Bit-disjointness criterion
nodes.statement: If $m-1$ and $n-1$ are not bit-disjoint, then $\trank(n,p,m)=\{p,p+1\}$, where two positive integers are bit-disjoint if there are no 1's in the same place of their binary notation.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors

nodes.name: Known formats with $\trank(n,p,m)=\{p,p+1\}$
nodes.statement: $\trank(n,p,m)=\{p,p+1\}$ in the following cases. \begin{enumerate} \item Both $m$ and $n$ are even. \item $m=5$ and $n\equiv 5,6,7,8\pmod 8$. \item $m=6$ and $n\equiv 2,4,5,6,7,8\pmod 8$. \item $m=7$ and $n\equiv 3,4,5,6,7,8\pmod 8$. \item $m=8$ and $n\equiv 2,3,4,5,6,7,8\pmod 8$. \item $m=9$ and $n\equiv 9,10,11,12,13,14,15,16\pmod {16}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Six families of $(m,n)$ (both even, or $m=5,\ldots,9$ with congruence conditions) already known to have two typical ranks.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors

nodes.name: $A''$, $A'$, $W_0$, $\rho$ and $\UUUUU$
nodes.statement: Set $ A''=(A_2;\cdots;A_{m-2};A_m;-A_{m-1};-A_{1})$. Then there is a permutation matrix $P\in\glin(u,\RRR)$ such that ${}_{p<}\fl_1(PA'')=-E_u$. Set $A'=PA''$ and $W_0=\fl_1(A')_{\leq p}$. Further set $\rho\colon\RRR^{u\times n\times m}\to\RRR^{u\times n\times m}$, $B=(B_1;\cdots;B_m)\mapsto P(B_2;\cdots;B_{m-2};B_m;-B_{m-1};-B_{1})$ and $\UUUUU=\mu^{-1}(\rho(\msUUU))$, where $\mu$ is the map defined in Definition \ref{def:sigma nu}. Then $\UUUUU$ is an open neighborhood of $W_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Permute and sign-flip the slices of $A$ to normalize ${}_{p<}\fl_1$, producing the base point $W_0$ and the neighborhood $\UUUUU=\mu^{-1}(\rho(\msUUU))$.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors

nodes.name: Proof of the count for $T\in\sigma^{-1}(\UUUUU)$
nodes.statement: Further, we see the following fact by Lemma \ref{lem:number gen}.
nodes.statement_short: Transport the count through $\mu\circ\sigma$.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors

nodes.name: Count of $[\psi(\aaa,\bbb)]$ for $T\in\sigma^{-1}(\UUUUU)$
nodes.statement: If $T\in\sigma^{-1}(\UUUUU)$, then $\#\{[\psi(\aaa,\bbb)]\in\PPP_\RRR\RRR^p\mid M(\aaa,\mu(\sigma(T)))\bbb=\zerovec, \aaa\in\RRR^m\setminus\{\zerovec\}, \bbb\in\RRR^n\setminus\{\zerovec\}\} =\alpha(m,n)$.
nodes.statement_short: The same $\alpha(m,n)$ count holds for tensors $T$ with $\sigma(T)\in\UUUUU$.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors

nodes.name: Proof that $\alpha(m,n)<p$ forces two typical ranks
nodes.statement: Since $\sigma^{-1}(\UUUUU)$ contains $\tau(W_0)$, $\sigma^{-1}(\UUUUU)$ is not an empty set. Therefore, we see by Lemma \ref{lem:rank p} that if $\alpha(m,n)<p$, then there exists a non-empty Euclidean open subset $\sigma^{-1}(\UUUUU)$ of $\RRR^{n\times p\times m}$ consisting of tensors of rank larger than $p$. Further, since we see by \cite[Theorem 8.1]{sms17} that typical ranks of $n\times p\times m$ tensors are less than or equal to $p+1$, we see the following fact.
nodes.statement_short: Non-emptiness of $\sigma^{-1}(\UUUUU)$ plus the rank-$p$ criterion gives an open set of rank $>p$; the upper bound $p+1$ comes from \cite{sms17}.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors

nodes.name: $\alpha(m,n)<p$ implies $\trank(n,p,m)=\{p,p+1\}$
nodes.statement: If $\alpha(m,n)<p$, then $\trank(n,p,m)=\{p,p+1\}$.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors

nodes.name: Main Theorem
nodes.statement: Suppose $3\leq m\leq n$ and $p=(m-1)(n-1)+1$. Then $\trank(n,p,m)=\{p,p+1\}$ in the following cases. \begin{enumerate} \item $m=3$ or $m=4$. \item $m=5$ and $n\leq 26$ or $n=28$. \item $m=6$ and $n\leq 34$. \item $m=7$ and $n\leq 16$. \item $m=8$ and $n\leq 16$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: For $p=(m-1)(n-1)+1$, $\trank(n,p,m)=\{p,p+1\}$ for $m\leq 4$ and for listed ranges of $n$ when $5\leq m\leq 8$.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors

nodes.name: Proof of the Main Theorem
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:alpha m n} and computation, we see that $\alpha(m,n)<p$ in the following cases: (1) $m=3$ or $m=4$, (2) $m=5$ and $n\leq 26$ or $n=28$, (3) $m=6$ and $n\leq 34$, (4) $m=7$ and $n\leq 12$, (5) $m=8$ and $n\leq 14$ and (6) $m=9$ and $n=10$. Thus, we see the result by Example \ref{ex:known} and Lemma \ref{lem:less than p}.
nodes.statement_short: Compute the cases where $\alpha(m,n)<p$ from the closed formula, then combine with the previously known cases.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors

nodes.name: Compute where $\alpha(m,n)<p$
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:alpha m n} and computation, we see that $\alpha(m,n)<p$ in the following cases: (1) $m=3$ or $m=4$, (2) $m=5$ and $n\leq 26$ or $n=28$, (3) $m=6$ and $n\leq 34$, (4) $m=7$ and $n\leq 12$, (5) $m=8$ and $n\leq 14$ and (6) $m=9$ and $n=10$.
nodes.statement_short: List the six $(m,n)$ families satisfying $\alpha(m,n)<p$.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors

nodes.name: Combine with the known cases
nodes.statement: Thus, we see the result by Example \ref{ex:known} and Lemma \ref{lem:less than p}.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude from the Example and the two-typical-ranks lemma.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors

nodes.name: The converse of the bit-disjointness fact fails
nodes.statement: Set $m=3$ and $n=5$. Then $m-1$ and $n-1$ are bit-disjoint. However, by Theorem \ref{thm:main}, we see that $\trank(n,p,m)=\{p,p+1\}$. Thus the converse of Fact \ref{fact:bit dis} does not valid.
nodes.statement_short: $m=3$, $n=5$ are bit-disjoint yet still have $\trank(n,p,m)=\{p,p+1\}$.
